structure_policy.notes: The authorial Chapter II location is preserved; analytical units inside this excerpt are reconstructed.

anchors.note: Objection from fallible practical judgment and utility
Reply: utility judgment also requires contestability

nodes.title: On Liberty, Chapter II (excerpt)
nodes.summary: Mill develops a fallibility-based defense of open discussion and answers an objection that practical judgment can justify suppressing harmful error.

nodes.title: First branch: suppression presumes infallibility
nodes.summary: The branch framing and first argument are treated as one unit: because suppressors are fallible, denying a hearing substitutes private certainty for absolute certainty.
nodes.role_in_parent: Combines the branch announcement with its first substantive argument.

nodes.title: Practical-duty objection
nodes.summary: A critic argues that fallible agents must nevertheless act and that socially useful beliefs may warrant protection.
nodes.role_in_parent: Challenges the fallibility argument by appealing to practical responsibility.

nodes.title: Utility does not escape contestability
nodes.summary: Mill argues that deciding usefulness is itself a disputable judgment and cannot bypass the need for open discussion.
nodes.role_in_parent: Answers the practical-duty and utility objection.

edges.explanation: The objection contests the inference from fallibility to a ban on suppressive action.
Mill directly answers the objection by showing that utility judgments do not avoid contestability.
The utility reply strengthens the fallibility-based case for allowing discussion.
